title: Don’t credit the LLM – Isaac Su
excerpt: Lately, an odd habit seems to have caught on among my peers when they’ve done something with an LLM.
content_html:
Lately, an odd habit seems to have caught on among my peers when they’ve done something with an LLM.

When asked “how many support requests have we received about the new Feature X?”, they answer “according to [LLM tool], we’ve received 17 requests since it was released.” When posting a pitch document or a pull request, they volunteer “I asked [LLM tool] to write this for me” or “[LLM tool] wrote the unit tests”.

Odd. Like a writer disclosing the spellchecker they used alongside every piece, or a pilot announcing their version of avionics software over the PA while taxiing to the runway.

Why did I need to know that?

At first, I put it down to a bit of novelty and excitement. But as this wore on, I started to wonder why someone might feel the need to declare their use of an LLM.

Perhaps:

  1. You believe in ascribing credit where credit is due. Using an LLM feels like cheating so disclosing it makes you feel less like an imposter for having produced something amazing.
  2. The LLM’s performance exceeded your wildest expectations, ergo the work is impressive by association. Never mind that it is only 80 percent complete and no one knows which 20 percent is missing.
  3. You outsourced the work to an LLM and didn’t bother to review it before hitting send. There may be mistakes but spotting them is left as an exercise for your recipients.
  4. LLM use has been mandated by Up Above. Claiming you’ve used one (even if you haven’t) buys you a higher tolerance for sloppiness since you are presumably facilitating your own eventual redundancy.

For 2 to 4, all I can say is I’m sorry and I hope things work out for you.

But for the first reason, I’d challenge the notion of sharing credit with a tool, let alone feeling like a cheat for using one. Credit and accountability are two sides of the same coin. A tool can only take as much credit as it can be held accountable for, so crediting it inadvertently dilutes your own accountability for the work.

If you’ve created something profound or remarkable, take complete credit for it. If it misses the mark or turns out to be utter slop, also take full responsibility and improve from there. This is how every meaningful or valuable thing was ever created long before the advent of “AI can make mistakes” and will remain so long after, with or without LLMs.

content_html_zh:
最近，当我的同事们用法学硕士做了一些事情时，似乎有一个奇怪的习惯在他们中间流行起来。

当被问及“我们收到了多少关于新功能 X 的支持请求？”时，他们回答“根据 [LLM 工具]，自发布以来我们已收到 17 个请求。” 在发布推介文件或拉取请求时，他们自愿“我要求[LLM工具]为我编写这个”或“[LLM工具]编写了单元测试”。

奇怪的。 就像作家披露他们在每一篇文章中使用的拼写检查器一样，或者飞行员在滑行到跑道时通过广播宣布他们的航空电子软件版本。

我为什么需要知道这一点？

起初，我把它归结为一点新奇和兴奋。 但随着时间的推移，我开始想知道为什么有人可能觉得有必要声明他们使用法学硕士。

也许：

  1. 你相信应得的功劳。 使用法学硕士感觉就像作弊，所以披露它会让你觉得自己不像一个冒名顶替者，因为你创造了一些令人惊叹的东西。
  2. 法学硕士的表现超出了你最疯狂的期望，因此这项工作令人印象深刻。 没关系，它只完成了 80%，而且没有人知道还缺少哪 20%。
  3. 您将工作外包给了法学硕士，并且在发送之前没有费心对其进行审查。 可能会有错误，但发现这些错误是留给收件人的练习。
  4. 法学硕士的使用已被 Up Below 强制要求。 声称你已经使用过一个（即使你没有）会让你对马虎行为有更高的容忍度，因为你可能会促进自己最终的裁员。

对于 2 到 4，我只能说对不起，希望你一切顺利。

但出于第一个原因，我会挑战与工具共享信用的概念，更不用说因为使用工具而感觉自己像个骗子。 信用和责任是同一枚硬币的两个方面。 一个工具只能获得与其负责的一样多的功劳，因此归功于它会无意中淡化你自己对工作的责任。

如果你创造了一些深刻或非凡的东西，就把它完全归功于它。 如果它没有达到目标或结果完全是马虎，也要承担全部责任并从那里改进。 这就是早在“人工智能会犯错误”出现之前，每一件有意义或有价值的东西就被创造出来的方式，并且在之后很长一段时间内，无论有没有法学硕士，它都将继续存在。
